title: Same-Letter Loop in a Grid
statement:
You get a grid of lowercase letters. From a cell you may step up, down, left or right to a neighbouring cell that holds the same letter.

Return true if some walk of length 4 or more starts and ends at the same cell, never steps straight back to the cell it just came from, and visits no other cell twice. In other words: is there a closed loop of one letter? Otherwise return false.

examples.why: The 2×2 block of a forms a loop of length 4.
The b cells form a plus shape. You can walk out and back, but stepping straight back is not allowed, so there is no loop.
The c cells form a ring of length 8 around the d.

constraints: grid[r][c] is a lowercase English letter
hints: Treat each cell as a node and connect neighbouring cells with the same letter. What is a loop in that graph?
It is a cycle in an undirected graph. In a grid every cycle already has length at least 4, so the length rule takes care of itself.
Add the edges one by one with union-find. If an edge joins two cells that are already connected, it closes a cycle.

explain.intuition:
Make a graph: cells are nodes, and two neighbouring cells with the same letter share an edge. The question becomes "does this undirected graph contain a cycle?". The "no stepping straight back" rule just says that going along an edge and back is not a cycle. And a grid has no triangles, so any real cycle has length 4 or more automatically.

Union-find detects a cycle neatly. Add the edges one at a time. Before adding an edge, ask whether its two cells are already in the same group. If they are, there was already a path between them, and this edge closes it into a loop. With 250 000 cells, this also avoids deep recursion.
steps: Give every cell an id r · cols + c and start union-find with each cell in its own group.
For each cell, look only right and down (so each edge is seen once).
If the neighbour has the same letter: if both cells already share a root, return true; otherwise union them.
If no edge closed a cycle, return false.
pitfalls: Treating the cell you just came from as a cycle. A DFS must skip its parent cell, or every edge looks like a loop.
Looking in all four directions with union-find. Each edge is then added twice, and the second time it falsely reports a cycle.
Recursive DFS on a 500×500 grid of one letter goes 250 000 calls deep and can overflow the stack.

complexity.time: O(R · C · α(R · C)), practically linear

solutions.title: Breadth-first search that remembers the parent
solutions.idea: Explore each same-letter region. Reaching an already visited cell that is not the one you came from means a cycle.

solutions.title: Union-find over same-letter edges
solutions.idea: Add each right and down edge between equal letters. An edge whose two cells are already connected closes a loop.

followups: Return the length of the shortest loop instead of just whether one exists.
Diagonal steps are now allowed too. Does the "length at least 4" rule still come for free?
